title: You may never work with an Elizabeth Holmes—but here's how to handle a co-worker who makes false claims
description: Elizabeth Holmes spent some of her last days out of prison with a film crew. She was trying, it seems, to clear her name."You really feel you did noth
body: Elizabeth Holmes spent some of her last days out of prison with a film crew. She was trying, it seems, to clear her name."You really feel you did nothing wrong?" Nathan Fielder, who co-directed the film "You Can See Everything," asks Holmes in the trailer. "I did not," she answers. Slated for theatrical release on Friday, the documentary had a surprise premiere at the Telluride Film Festival in September that brought Holmes back into the public eye. Holmes built the now-dissolved blood-testing company Theranos to a multi-billion-dollar valuation and assembled a luminary-filled board of directors on the back of revolutionary promises, some of which never materialized. She was convicted on multiple counts of fraud in 2022 and sentenced to 135 months, or more than 11 years, in prison. She argued in her trial defense that she believed Theranos' fledgling technology worked. In a Sept. 27 post on X, Holmes doubled down, writing: "I am fighting to prove my innocence."Though it's impossible to see inside someone's head, onlookers have debated over the years whether Holmes was sincere in believing her own outlandish claims. You may never work with someone as infamous and enigmatic as Holmes. But how do you handle a co-worker who appears to believe their own false statements? They might be charming, charismatic and earnest. You, and others, might desperately want to believe what they're saying. But when a pattern starts to emerge, you can't ignore it, because you could be left holding the bag when things unravel. I've consulted for major companies including Google and Microsoft, and taught executive education for more than a decade at Columbia Business School and Duke University's Fuqua School of Business. I've seen how difficult it can be to deal with a colleague who just can't seem to be straight with you, whether they never deliver their work as promised or constantly misrepresent situations. When you don't have the power to personally remove them from their position, you have to find creative workarounds, so you can get your own job done. Here are five strategies you can use when you're dealing with a co-worker who seems a little delusional. 1. Separate the person from the behavior One of the most confusing parts about having a co-worker behave this way is that you might genuinely like them. It often feels inspiring to be around people who have a vision and a can-do attitude. That energy can mobilize a team around big goals and lead to genuine progress, even if you don't hit your boldest targets. But it's helpful only up to a point. A repeated pattern of unrealistic expectations and broken promises damages trust and hurts your entire organization. You don't have to see the person as a villain to recognize that their behavior is causing problems.2. Build in a margin of error Think back to the promises your colleague has made to you, write them down and compare them to the outcome. Did they promise to get you a report and then deliver it a week late without apologizing or even acknowledging they missed the deadline? Did they assure you they were on track for 100 new customers by the end of the quarter and only deliver 25 without explanation?Look for patterns in their over- or under-estimations. Are they inaccurate about speed, volume or sentiment? With that data in mind, you can begin to translate what they're telling you to create your own, more realistic estimates. If they tell you something will be ready in a month, you'll know to plan for two. Their wild overconfidence won't cause downstream problems for your team, because you'll already be prepared.As you do this exercise for yourself, start documenting. Keep track of communications and outcomes that don't match in case you need them later to escalate the situation up to your boss, leadership or HR.  3. Create checkpointsThe problems that affect you most are the ones you never saw coming. It's hard to pivot last-minute when you're blindsided by unforeseen developments. So put a monitoring system in place to avoid surprises, as much as possible, from an unpredictable colleague. If you're working on a joint project, identify checkpoints when you'll establish where things really are. For instance, if your co-worker promised you a prototype in six weeks, you can create a checklist of milestones ranging from "customer surveys" to "design mockups" to "sourcing materials" to "fabrication of device."If they're assuring you everything is on track at week four, but no design mockups have even been created, it's reasonable to assume they'll miss the deadline — and you can prepare now, rather than scrambling later. But ultimately, there are only so many ways you can personally compensate for a colleague's poor performance or broken promises. The next step is to involve others. 4. Get external supportWhen someone is feeding you inaccurate information one-on-one, they can pretend you misunderstood. That's much harder to do when there are witnesses. Actively involve your manager or co-workers in planning sessions so that any commitments are made publicly, and your manager can handle follow-up and accountability. Your colleague might think twice about making grandiose promises if they understand that a failure will be visible to everyone. But sometimes, even the risk of public embarrassment isn't enough to stop them. 5. Escalate and extricate yourself You probably don't have the authority to fire your co-worker, and it can be tricky to actively try to get them fired. Rather than pushing for their ouster — and risking their wrath if they find out — you can concentrate on a different goal you have much more control over: limiting your dependence on them. Because you've already involved your manager, by now they're well aware of that person's shortcomings. So they won't be surprised, and will likely be sympathetic, when you come to them and say: "I need your help. My team has been delayed three times because Jeremy told us he'd have the mockups ready, and it hasn't happened. It's unsustainable for us to rely on him. Can we think creatively about how to ensure my team's work is able to proceed?" There are at least three potential outcomes:You'll get support for a creative solution. Let's say your boss can't fire the hypothetical Jeremy either, whether it's because he's outside their chain of command or because he has "protected status" in the organization as the protege of a top leader. But your boss will want to help you get your own work done, so they might let you partner with outside vendors or bring in a new team member to work around Jeremy. Your co-worker will get fired. Alternatively, it's possible your appraisal may be the evidence your boss wants and needs to make the case that Jeremy should go, and they'll be grateful you provided the impetus. You've protected yourself. If your boss literally can't do anything, you've at least flagged the problem so that any future failures will be contextualized — "of course, they were relying on Jeremy" — rather than seen as your own inability to deliver. It's incredibly challenging to deal with a colleague who seems to believe their own false claims. But these strategies will help you avoid getting dragged down when their lies and exaggerations are finally discovered.Dorie Clark taught executive education for more than a decade at Columbia Business School and Duke University's Fuqua School of Business. She is a keynote speaker, former presidential campaign spokeswoman, and bestselling author of "The Long Game." You can subscribe to her e-newsletter here.

title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang urges U.S.-China dialogue on 'potentially dangerous' AI
description: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said the chipmaker "absolutely must" work with Chinese AI companies on monitoring risks around the "potentially dangerous" tec
body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said the chipmaker "absolutely must" work with Chinese AI companies on monitoring risks around the "potentially dangerous" technology."We absolutely should work with each other so that we advance the technology safely," he told CNBC during a media briefing on Wednesday evening in London. Discussions around AI safety have intensified in recent months, after researchers from AI labs including OpenAI and Anthropic called for a slowdown in developing the tech and warned of existential risks to humanity. While OpenAI's Sam Altman and Anthropic's Dario Amodei have called for greater regulation, Huang has emerged as a prominent voice in opposition to that view. Huang said that "dialogue" was the way to work with Chinese AI companies, adding that he has "dialogues with many of the researchers in China.""We ought to enhance the dialogue," he added. "The United States should do it... I advocated that the U.K. do the same thing."U.S.-China AI cooperationAI safety has become a key topic between the U.S. and Chinese governments, with both countries weighing how to address the risks posed by the rapidly advancing tech. Prior to U.S. President Donald Trump's meeting with Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent discussed the prospect of a "U.S.-China AI dialogue" with his Chinese counterpart, He Lifeng, in September, including a channel for incidents "up to a national security level."A Chinese readout of the meeting said President Xi pointed out that China and the U.S. "may have competition, but they may cooperate even more" in AI. "The two sides can continue their dialogue on AI, exchange views on its risks and benefits, and jointly prevent the misuse and abuse of AI," Xi said, per the readout.Huang said that the U.K. is in a position "in the world to be able to be a convener of many of these dialogues" related to AI, because of the country's "intellectual capital."

schema.headline: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang urges U.S.-China dialogue on 'potentially dangerous' AI

title: TSMC posts record profit for a sixth straight quarter, beating estimates on AI boom
description: A TSMC logo is displayed on a wall in Hsinchu, Taiwan April 15, 2025. Ann Wang | ReutersTaiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. on Thursday reported a
body: A TSMC logo is displayed on a wall in Hsinchu, Taiwan April 15, 2025. Ann Wang | ReutersTaiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. on Thursday reported a record third-quarter profit that beat estimates, powered by an unrelenting global appetite for AI chips.Here are TSMC's third-quarter results against LSEG SmartEstimates, which are weighted toward forecasts from analysts who are more consistently accurate:Revenue: 1.49 trillion new Taiwan dollars ($46.36 billion)  vs. NT$1.47 trillion Net Income: NT$763.1 billion vs. NT$746.34 billion expected The world's largest contract chipmaker posted a record net profit for a sixth straight quarter, reporting 68.7% surge in the reported quarter from a year earlier.  TSMC's third-quarter operating margin came in at 58.7%, exceeding the upper end of its guidance range of 58%, showcasing the pricing power enjoyed by the company as the AI boom fuels demand for semiconductors. TSMC forecast fourth-quarter revenue between $52.3 billion and $54.3 billion, representing a 14% sequential increase and a 58% jump from a year earlier at the midpoint of its guidance range, according to the company's earnings call. The chipmaker expects its capital expenditure from 2026 to 2028 to be significantly higher than in the previous three years, as it continues to ramp up investments to support growing customer demand.TSMC's stronger-than-expected results and upgraded full-year revenue outlook underscore how demand for advanced chips continues to outpace its production capacity, with the company's elevated capital spending reflecting confidence in sustained growth over the coming years, Sravan Kundojjala, an analyst at SemiAnalysis, told CNBC via email.TSMC expects its fourth-quarter business to be supported by continued strong demand for its advanced chipmaking technologies, including the ramp-up of its 2-nanometer process.Kundojjala also highlighted TSMC's careful approach to capacity expansion, adding that the chipmaker is assessing whether customers have the financing and supporting components needed to deploy AI systems."Even after those checks, TSMC says demand remains well above its supply capacity," he said, adding that it reinforces confidence in the AI buildout while ensuring investment decisions reflect customers' ability to deploy the chips they order.Advanced technologies, defined as 7-nanometer and more advanced technologies, made up for 79% of TSMC's total wafer revenue in the reported. The 3-nanometer chips accounted for the largest share of its revenue in the third quarter at 33%, followed by 5- and 7-nanometer chips.By platform, high-performance computing accounted for the largest share of revenue at 68%, followed by smartphones at 21%. Meanwhile, automotive was the fastest-growing segment on a quarter-on-quarter basis, with 23%  growth rate.TSMC said demand for AI chips remains strong, driven by the growing adoption of agentic AI and open-source AI models, which are expected to make AI more accessible and fuel demand for advanced semiconductors.The company's free cash flow surged to NT$476.56 billion in the third quarter, from NT$139.38 billion a year ago. TSMC also pointed to rising demand for AI accelerators, processors used in agentic AI applications and networking, adding that semiconductors are set to play an increasingly important role in the global AI supply chain. TSMC also said it had completed construction of its second fab in Arizona and is installing equipment, with mass production expected to begin in the third quarter of 2027, slightly ahead of its previous schedule.TSMC board approved NT$7.00 cash dividend for the second quarter. During its second-quarter earnings announcement in July, TSMC had outlined plans to expand its U.S. manufacturing footprint, including a total planned investment of $265 billion in Arizona.  The chipmaker is also reportedly considering expanding beyond Arizona, evaluating a potential investment in Texas as it looks to further strengthen its U.S. manufacturing presence.

schema.headline: TSMC posts record profit for a sixth straight quarter, beating estimates on AI boom

title: Elon Musk says Trump is 'ultimately' responsible for any curbs on Ukraine's Starshield systems
description: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk attends a meeting with US President Donald Trump and technology executives about artificial intelligence in the East Room of the
body: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk attends a meeting with US President Donald Trump and technology executives about artificial intelligence in the East Room of the White House in Washington, DC, on Sept. 29, 2026. Kent Nishimura | AFP | Getty ImagesSpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk said Wednesday that the U.S. government and President Donald Trump are responsible for any curbs on Ukraine's military-grade Starlink network.Writing on X, Musk said that "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS."Ukraine had accused SpaceX of imposing new restrictions on the Starshield internet service without warning, leading to disruptions to Ukrainian military operations amid fresh Russian strikes on its energy infrastructure. On Wednesday, Serhii Beskrestnov, an advisor to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on defense technology, said SpaceX had implemented a speed limit on Starlink terminals in motion, without notifying the country's defense forces. That had disrupted some missions, and the same restrictions also applied to Starshield, he said on Telegram. Starlink is used to operate Ukraine's interceptor drones, the "most effective solution" against Moscow's Shahed drones, Beskrestnov said. Starshield is a military-grade satellite network, while Starlink is only meant for "civilian or defensive activities," Musk said. Some restrictions appear to have been partially lifted, with former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov thanking Musk early Thursday morning that Starlink connectivity at speeds of up to 160 kilometers an hour had been restored. "Removing Starshield's speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine's defense," Fedorov added. The developments come amid tensions between Kyiv and Washington over an "energy ceasefire," between Ukraine and Russia announced by U.S. President Donald Trump. Ukraine has, however, welcomed a deal subject to Moscow honoring its commitment, while Russian authorities said talks were ongoing, without confirming whether they had reached an agreement. On Monday, Zelenskyy accused the Russians of breaching the ceasefire. Trump had also taken aim at Ukraine as it continues to strike Russian energy facilities, saying that Kyiv's attacks were responsible for the increase in diesel prices, instead of the U.S.' war with Iran. Washington has threatened to cut intelligence sharing with Kyiv, Reuters reported Wednesday, while Ukrainian officials said a day earlier that they have not received warnings of Russian attacks on the country for two straight days.— CNBC's Elsa Olhen contributed to this report.

schema.headline: Elon Musk says Trump is 'ultimately' responsible for any curbs on Ukraine's Starshield systems

title: Bank of America hired 1,000 contractors to patch software flaws exposed by Anthropic's Mythos
description: watch nowBank of America has hired an army of external contractors to help it patch software vulnerabilities exposed by advanced artificial intelligen
body: watch nowBank of America has hired an army of external contractors to help it patch software vulnerabilities exposed by advanced artificial intelligence models including Anthropic's Mythos, the bank's CEO, Brian Moynihan, told CNBC on Wednesday.In an interview after the bank's third-quarter earnings release, Moynihan said that earlier this year the company rushed to bolster a wide spectrum of its internal and vendor code using thousands of employees and outside personnel. "That risk is real risk, and that's why when the frontier-type models came out. … A lot of us sat down and said, 'How do we figure out how to get through this quickly?" Moynihan told CNBC's Leslie Picker."We put on 1,000 contractors to help us do the patching work in the second quarter, and those people remain here today, helping us, on top of the 3,000 people we have in that area," he said.The bank spent a "couple hundred million plus" on the software remediation and regulatory issues related to anti-money laundering compliance in the third quarter, Moynihan told analysts earlier Wednesday. The comments are some of the first by a major U.S. corporation to specify the manpower and dollars spent to protect software systems from Mythos, which was released to a small group of banks, technology firms and government agencies in April.They also highlight the dual-edged nature of AI: While it can help companies save money by boosting productivity, the ability of models like Mythos to uncover and exploit decades-old software flaws has also forced firms into a costly defensive scramble. "We've got to stay ahead of them, and we've got to be mindful that the people doing the software development are the people trying to sell us the services," Moynihan said.Still, Moynihan — speaking as his company's shares slumped as much as 8% Wednesday — sought to reassure investors that the spending increase was temporary. "Once you patch, you don't have to patch as much. … The pipeline moves through," Moynihan said, adding that the bank expects remediation costs to decline over time.In other places, AI is helping to reduce expenses. Bank of America has about 130 internal AI projects, and savings from those efforts are expected to rise from $300 million this year to $700 million in 2027, Moynihan told analysts. Bank of America's head count fell by about 3,400 employees in the past year as the firm cut roughly 5% of managers, he said. It's unclear how much of that workforce reduction is attributable to AI.

schema.headline: Bank of America hired 1,000 contractors to patch software flaws exposed by Anthropic's Mythos

title: Banks with Jeffrey Epstein ties eyed by Democrats Warren and Garcia
description: Ranking member Rep. Robert Garcia (D-CA) (L), and Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA).Anna Moneymaker | Getty ImagesFinancial institutions and bank executive
body: Ranking member Rep. Robert Garcia (D-CA) (L), and Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA).Anna Moneymaker | Getty ImagesFinancial institutions and bank executives that may have aided the late financier Jeffrey Epstein's sex trafficking operation are in the sights of a bipartisan group of lawmakers. Legislation introduced Thursday — and led by Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif. — would require financial regulators to produce records related to Epstein, compel those regulators to investigate banks and executives with ties to the deceased convicted sex offender, and require industry bans and civil penalties for those found to have aided him."I have spent the last year calling on Donald Trump's financial regulators to launch investigations into the big banks and executives who may have enabled Jeffrey Epstein's horrific crimes," Warren, who leads the Senate banking committee, said in a statement. "Since they have failed to act, Congress must. The bipartisan Epstein Wall Street Records Act will ensure overdue accountability for the wealthy and well-connected on Wall Street who put profits over people." The legislation is co-led in the House by Reps. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., Thomas Massie, R-Ky., and Raja Krishnamoorthi, D-Ill. Sens. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., Ron Wyden, D-Ore., and Ben Ray Lujan, D-N.M., signed on to the Senate version. The house version has 17 Democratic co-sponsors.The proposal would apply to the Federal Reserve, Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, Treasury's Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Securities and Exchange Commission. None of the regulators immediately responded to a request for comment.

schema.headline: Banks with Jeffrey Epstein ties eyed by Democrats Warren and Garcia

title: Lisa Cook lawyer doubts Trump committee's fairness as president calls her 'automatic no vote'
description: Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook and attorney Abbe Lowell leave the U.S. Supreme Court in Washington, Jan. 21, 2026.Kevin Dietsch | Getty ImagesAn a
body: Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook and attorney Abbe Lowell leave the U.S. Supreme Court in Washington, Jan. 21, 2026.Kevin Dietsch | Getty ImagesAn attorney for Lisa Cook voiced strong doubts that President Donald Trump's committee investigating mortgage fraud allegations against the Federal Reserve governor would be fair and objective.The lawyer, Abbe Lowell, said the committee is plagued by issues that undermine the appearance of the Fed's independence, including "demonstrably biased members" and "unspecified additional allegations" against Cook.Those and other issues "would have to be addressed before a hearing could occur" in the probe, Lowell wrote in a letter sent Tuesday to Will Scharf, Trump's aide and counsel. No such hearing could take place until at least December, weeks later than the initially scheduled date, Lowell insisted.The letter came three days after Trump slammed Cook as "dishonest" and griped that she was an "automatic no vote" — apparently referring to her opposition to cutting interest rates, which the president strongly desires.Cook last voted to cut rates in December 2025, siding with the majority. The Fed unanimously voted to raise rates after its most recent meeting in September."She shouldn't be in an important position," Trump said of Cook in those remarks to reporters after returning from a rally in Tennessee on Saturday.White House spokesman Matthew Middleton said in response to Lowell's letter that Trump "is performing his constitutional duty in evaluating Lisa Cook's conduct and eligibility to continue serving as a governor on the Federal Reserve.""The Constitution charges the President with ensuring that the laws are faithfully executed and that the conduct of members of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System is above reproach," Middleton said in a statement.An in-person hearing at the White House is currently scheduled for Nov. 5, according to Trump's Oct. 7 presidential memo establishing the "committee of inquiry" into Cook.Cook's lawyers did not immediately rule out participating in that hearing, and in fact said the Fed governor "welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name," despite their concerns.But in Tuesday's letter, Lowell said Cook cannot attend a hearing on Nov. 5 because she "will be executing her official duties as Governor at financial and monetary policy meetings in Europe."After that, Cook will immediately start preparing for the next meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee in early December, Lowell said.The White House did not immediately respond when asked by CNBC if the scheduled hearing would be moved in light of Cook's alleged scheduling conflicts. Lowell also said he needs time to speak with Cook about issues raised by the White House's most recent correspondence, as well as to prepare her for any possible hearing, "which, because of her being in Asia on Federal Reserve duties, cannot be done until she returns.""With all of that (and court hearings I have scheduled in November), the earliest date for any hearing would need to be in December following the FOMC meeting," Lowell wrote Scharf.Trump established the three-member committee two months after reviving his long-running effort to fire Cook, an appointee of former President Joe Biden, from the central bank's board of governors.The Supreme Court in late June blocked Trump's first attempt to remove Cook, ruling that she was not given sufficient due process under federal law. But that decision did not stop Trump from trying again.Middleton said in his statement, "The President is going beyond what the Supreme Court required by offering Lisa Cook an in-person hearing that will be conducted in a fair and open process."But Lowell wrote Tuesday, "We have significant concerns regarding the objectivity and fitness of the committee," which comprises three executive branch officials, including top Trump economic aide Kevin Hassett.Hassett "already has publicly insinuated that the President has 'cause' to fire Governor Cook," Lowell noted, citing the economic advisor's comments from August 2025. Hassett in those remarks also accused Cook of "making a partisan stance contrary to the independence of the Fed" by refusing to step aside while a Justice Department investigation played out into the mortgage fraud allegations, which Cook denies.The comments suggest Hassett has already prejudged the case, Lowell told Scharf, "surely belying your assertion that the 'hearing' as proposed would be 'substantive and fair.'""A hearing with demonstrably biased members, unspecified additional allegations, and an unclear schedule for the disclosure of any additional evidence – with no explanation for why it was not previously produced – is not a process that respects the appearance or history of independence," Lowell wrote.

schema.headline: Lisa Cook lawyer doubts Trump committee's fairness as president calls her 'automatic no vote'

title: Wholesale prices jumped 6.3% annually in September, biggest gain since 2022
description: September's producer price index came in much hotter than economists forecast on Thursday, underscoring the continued inflationary pressure from energ
body: September's producer price index came in much hotter than economists forecast on Thursday, underscoring the continued inflationary pressure from energy amid the U.S. war with Iran.The measure of underlying inflation pressures climbed 1.3% in September and 6.3% on an annual basis, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. That marked the largest monthly and annual gains since March 2022 and December 2022, respectively.Both readings topped expectations of economists polled by Dow Jones, who forecast an advance of 0.6% on the month and 5.5% annually.Energy drove a sizable chunk of those increases as the Middle East conflict curtailed oil supply and sent prices surging. The so-called core PPI, which excludes volatile food and energy prices from the wholesaler inflation index, added 0.7% on the month and 5% over the 12-month period.But there are signs that soaring energy prices are having downstream effects on other categories. The BLS said in Thursday's release that almost half of September's increase in processed goods for immediate demand was connected to the rise in diesel fuel prices.It's the latest report in recent days showing that inflation continues to hit consumers and companies.Wednesday's consumer price index release showed a rise of 0.6% from August to September and 3.7% on a 12-month basis. Economists polled by Dow Jones had forecast growth of 0.6% and 3.6%, respectively.Excluding food and energy, the core CPI added 0.3% on the month and 2.6% compared with a year ago. Economists anticipated increases of 0.2% and 2.5%, respectively.Wednesday's Beige Book, a chronicle of economic activity published by the Federal Reserve, had the highest number of mentions of terms related to inflation on record, according to an analysis from Bespoke Investment Group.Retail sales grew 0.8% in September, surpassing the rate of 0.4% anticipated by economists, according to government data released in a separate report Thursday. That marked a slowdown from a month prior, when retail sales rose by more than 1%.Excluding spending on autos and gas stations, retail sales increased 0.25% from August to September, a drop from around 1.1% in the prior period. This slowdown offers a sign that high prices related to fuel are causing consumers to tighten the belt elsewhere.This week's data has left a growing minority of fed funds futures traders expecting the central bank to raise rates at its meeting later this month. Traders are now pricing in a nearly 34% likelihood that the Fed hikes borrowing costs on Oct. 28, up from under 18% a week prior, according to CME's FedWatch tool. About 90% expect at least one hike by the end of the year."With a second day in a row of higher-than-expected inflation numbers, it seems the Fed will have no choice but to raise rates again this year," said Chris Zaccarelli, investing chief at Northlight Asset Management.These reports offer some of the final insights into the pace of inflation in the U.S. ahead of the midterm election, which could impact how much power each political party has in Washington.

schema.headline: Wholesale prices jumped 6.3% annually in September, biggest gain since 2022

title: Trump says Nidal Hasan execution won't be livestreamed
description: Nidal Hasan, charged with killing 13 people and wounding 32 in a November 2009 shooting spree at Fort Hood, Texas, is pictured in an undated Bell Coun
body: Nidal Hasan, charged with killing 13 people and wounding 32 in a November 2009 shooting spree at Fort Hood, Texas, is pictured in an undated Bell County Sheriff's Office photograph.Bell County Sheriff's Office | ReutersPresident Donald Trump said Thursday that the planned execution by firing squad of convicted Fort Hood mass killer Nidal Hasan would not be livestreamed, as the Pentagon had planned.Trump's announcement came after growing backlash against plans to show the former U.S. Army major's execution live online, with concern that the footage would become a recruiting tool for terrorists. Hasan, who is paralyzed from the waist down, is scheduled to be executed at 1 p.m. Central Time time on Dec. 3 in Fort Hood, which is located in Killeen, Texas. Hasan could seek to delay the execution with a new legal challenge."Nidal Malik Hasan, a former U.S. Army Major turned traitor, is a very bad and evil man," Trump said in a Truth Social post, noting that Hasan had killed 13 people — one of whom was pregnant — and injured 32 others in the Nov. 5, 2009, shooting spree."With all of that being said, I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan but, many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device," Trump wrote."He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed.""That said, the execution may be viewed in person by the immediate families of the victims, if they so choose," Trump wrote. "They deserve to witness JUSTICE!"Hours before Trump's announcement, a Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll was released and showed that 80% of Americans said the execution should not be streamed live, versus just 18% who supported the idea. About 52% of Americans support Hasan being executed, according to the poll of 2,545 U.S. adults, which had a margin of error of plus or minus two percentage points.On Monday, Archbishop Timothy Broglio, who leads the Catholic Archdiocese for Military Services, issued a statement saying that any Catholics assigned to the firing squad should "request to be excused from this action contrary to the teaching of the Church."The Pentagon on Oct. 5 said that Trump had approved a recommendation by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to have Hasan, 56, executed by a U.S. Army firing squad. Presidential approval is required for executions of military executions under the Uniform Code of Military Justice.Hasan would be the first member of the U.S. military executed by firing squad since World War II.Hegseth on Oct. 8 said the execution would be at Fort Hood and, "He's going to get a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be.""And we'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public, because people need to understand that ... there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said.The Pentagon later said it would be livestreamed.Before Trump's announcement Thursday that the livestream would not happen, it was unclear which major video-streaming platforms, if any, would have aired the execution.The Verge reported last week that YouTube, Twitch, Meta and X did not respond when asked if they would allow the execution on their sites, while TikTok pointed to the company's policies barring "shocking and graphic content."Vice President JD Vance raised doubts last week about whether the livestream is "actually going to happen," saying he would not watch it if it did."So whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don't forget that this is the guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people," Vance said. "Now, that said, if it's ultimately livestreamed, I'm not going to be watching it."Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., last week said in a post on X that the idea of livestreaming the execution was "beyond disgusting.""Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do," Tillis tweeted. "It should not be happening in America."Former Army Sgt. Alonzo Lunsford, whom Hasan shot seven times during the attack, said he opposed the execution being livestreamed even as he said he planned to attend it in person."I want to be in the room where I can see him, and he can see me," Lunsford said last week, according to CBS News. "People have to be held accountable for their sins, but I don't want this to be some pay-per-view event, like some John Wick movie.""As a country, we're better than that."Archbishop Paul Coakley, president of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops, condemned the plan to show the execution publicly. "Our God is the God of life. In no way can Hassan's actions be condoned but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered. The word of God exhorts us: 'do not repay anyone evil for evil,'" Coakley said, quoting St. Paul's Letter to the Romans."The public execution even of one who has done grave harm will only further undermine the moral fabric of our nation and be a blight on the conscience of its people," Coakley said.Hasan was convicted and sentenced to death after a 2013 court-martial.His execution would be the first carried out by the U.S. military since 1961. That year, Army Pvt. John Bennett was hanged at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas, for the rape and attempted murder of a girl in Austria.CNBC has reached out to the Pentagon for comment on Trump's post. Nader Hasan, a cousin of Nidal who had spoken out after the Fort Hood shooting, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

title: U.S. reportedly considers use of 'mother of all bombs' as Iran vows to fight on
description: A U.S. Department of Defense (DoD) handout photo shows the Massive Ordinance Air Blast (MOAB) weapon on March 11, 2003 at Eglin Air Force Base, Florid
body: A U.S. Department of Defense (DoD) handout photo shows the Massive Ordinance Air Blast (MOAB) weapon on March 11, 2003 at Eglin Air Force Base, Florida.Usaf | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesThe U.S. military has drawn up options for renewed strikes on Iran that include the potential use of one of the biggest nonnuclear bombs in its arsenal, CNN reported Thursday, as Tehran vowed to continue fighting for its demands. The strike plans involve the possible use of the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb, nicknamed the "mother of all bombs," CNN reported, citing multiple U.S. officials familiar with the matter. CNBC has not independently confirmed the report. An official told CNBC the Defense Department "plans for a wide range of operational scenarios to execute Presidential and Secretary level direction and to ensure mission success in any operational environment." The 21,600-pound airburst weapon is designed to affect surface targets over a wide area and has so far not been deployed by the U.S. in previous strikes on targets inside Iran. It was used in Afghanistan in 2017 during the previous Trump administration. U.S. President Donald Trump said last week that he would not order a resumption of military strikes before the midterm elections on Nov. 3. Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said in a televised address late Wednesday that Iran must continue to use a combination of military and defensive capabilities, negotiations, and regional strategic leverage to push the U.S. to accept its demands. Officials in Tehran have previously listed demands including Washington lifting its naval blockade and sanctions and withdrawing U.S. military forces from the region.Ghalibaf said Tehran's goal is not to be locked in an endless war, but to prevent the U.S. and its other adversaries from being able to achieve their own objectives through military attacks, Iranian state-affiliated media reported.

schema.headline: U.S. reportedly considers use of 'mother of all bombs' as Iran vows to fight on

title: Treasury yields slide as investors flee to safety of bonds amid tech rout
description: A trader works on the floor at the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York City, U.S., Sept. 16, 2026.Jeenah Moon | ReutersTreasury yields dropped
body: A trader works on the floor at the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York City, U.S., Sept. 16, 2026.Jeenah Moon | ReutersTreasury yields dropped Thursday, as investors continued to cash in technology shares and fled to the safety of bonds following the latest wholesale inflation data.The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield recently tumbled almost 13 basis points to 5.066%, as did the 30-year Treasury bond yield, to 5.40%. The 2-year Treasury note yield was down more than 6 basis points, to 4.74%. One basis point equals to 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.Wholesale prices jumped at an annual rate of 6.3% in September, the biggest gain since 2022, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Economists polled by Dow Jones were forecasting an advance of 5.5%.The producer price report comes on the heels of the latest consumer price index released Wednesday that also came in hotter than expected. The measure of goods and services costs across the U.S. economy rose 0.6% monthly and 3.7% on an annual basis in September against the consensus forecast for gains of 0.6% and 3.6%, respectively. Investors rotated into bonds amid a broader flight to safety, as growing fears of higher inflation and interest rates, and their effect on the AI spending boom, saw investors dump shares of high-flying technology companies. The data did little to change interest rate expectations, with fed funds futures pricing in at least one more quarter-point raise by the end of the year, according to the CME FedWatch tool. The likelihood that rates will move higher than the current fed funds range of 3.75% to 4.00% has risen sharply over the past month."With a second day in a row of higher-than-expected inflation numbers, it seems the Fed will have no choice but to raise rates again this year," said Chris Zaccarelli, chief investment officer at Northlight Asset Management. "While we don't expect them to raise rates later this month (because it is so close to the mid-term election), we do think that they will increase the Fed Funds rate another [quarter point] in December."Last month, the U.S. central bank raised benchmark lending rates for the first time this year, lifting fed funds from their prior range of 3.50% to 3.75%.Correction: A previous version of this article misstated how traders are pricing the Fed's next interest rate decision.

title: Ukraine to resume strikes on Russian refineries, shattering hopes of an 'energy ceasefire'
description: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said Ukraine will resume attacks on Russian energy infrastructure after Moscow failed to uphold its end of an "energ
body: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said Ukraine will resume attacks on Russian energy infrastructure after Moscow failed to uphold its end of an "energy ceasefire" deal proposed by President Donald Trump. "The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We're done," Zelenskyy told the Financial Times after Ukraine paused strikes on energy targets for three days at the request of Washington.On Sunday, Trump announced an "energy ceasefire" between Ukraine and Russia in an effort to put an end to the countries attacking each other's power facilities and thereby lower the price of oil and diesel ahead of the U.S. midterm elections next month.Despite Ukraine's pause, officials in Kyiv said the country has been stripped of advance warnings of incoming ballistic missiles, as Starlink connectivity services had been restricted across the country, disrupting military operations. The restrictions apply to the sister service Starshield. Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Zelenskyy on defense technology, said Wednesday that SpaceX has implemented a speed limit on Starlink terminals in motion without notifying Ukrainian defense forces. "It is clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is related to the current political situation," Beskrestnov said on Telegram.watch nowAccording to SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, the U.S. government is ultimately responsible for any curbs on Ukraine's military-grade Starlink network. "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government," he wrote on X on Wednesday.The White House and SpaceX didn't respond to CNBC's request for comment. In an interview with Piers Morgan released late Wednesday, Zelenskyy said he felt let down by Trump's recent dealings with Vladimir Putin, Russia's attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure and the apparent speed limits imposed on SpaceX's military communications network Starshield.Asked whether he felt "betrayed by what has been happening," Zelenskyy answered: "Really, yes," but stressed that Ukraine's survival and its strategic relationship with the U.S. mattered more than his personal emotions. Zelenskyy said Ukraine had honored a proposed energy ceasefire for three days, refraining from both attacks and retaliation, while Russia subsequently launched a massive assault on Ukrainian energy infrastructure, including approximately 40 ballistic missiles. He said he had warned U.S. officials that Russia would violate the ceasefire and described the reported Starlink shutdown as an "absolutely crazy" move that was not consistent with the behavior expected between partners.

schema.headline: Ukraine to resume strikes on Russian refineries, shattering hopes of an 'energy ceasefire'

title: Amazon launches new Bee 'personal AI' devices that listen to conversations
description: Amazon's Bee Frontier device can be worn on a wrist or clipped on to clothing.AmazonAmazon on Thursday unveiled two new Bee listening devices, includi
body: Amazon's Bee Frontier device can be worn on a wrist or clipped on to clothing.AmazonAmazon on Thursday unveiled two new Bee listening devices, including a wearable and a credit card-sized voice recorder, marking its latest push into the AI gadget market.  The Bee Frontier is an upgraded version of Amazon's existing wearable that can either be worn on a wrist or clipped to clothing. Similar to earlier generations, the Bee Frontier has up to seven days of battery life, but it's also more expensive, costing $75 compared with its $50 predecessor. Amazon acquired Bee, a San Francisco startup known for its always-listening bracelet, in July 2025 for an undisclosed amount. Bee bracelets are equipped with artificial intelligence and microphones that can record, transcribe and analyze conversations.   The dual mics on the Bee Frontier have upgraded noise filtering, "so it can take note of what matters and ignore what doesn't, even in noisy environments like a crowded restaurant or open office," Amazon said in a blog post.Amazon also debuted the $100 Bee Eclipse, which functions like other Bee devices, but instead of being worn, the credit card-sized gadget magnetically snaps on to the back of a smartphone. The Bee Frontier is available Thursday, while the Bee Eclipse "will be available soon," the company said. Amazon is refreshing its Bee lineup as tech companies gear up for the holiday season with a slew of new AI hardware. Amazon nixed its budget-friendly Fire family of tablets in favor of three new AI-infused Alexa Tablets, while Microsoft showcased an Nvidia-powered Windows laptop and Apple unveiled its HomeView smart home hub with Siri AI. The Bee gadgets will compete with other AI wearables already on the market. The $100 Bee Eclipse is a credit card-sized device that magnetically snaps on to the back of a smartphone.Meta has seen growing momentum from its smart glasses that are infused with AI and have a built-in camera. The glasses have also generated widespread privacy and civil rights concerns from users, advocacy groups and lawmakers. Meta has also announced a palm-sized pendant called Muse Charm that runs its latest Muse AI assistant. Plaud developed a card-shaped note-taking device, and Friend offers an AI necklace. Amazon's voice-activated Echo smart speaker got users comfortable with interacting with its Alexa AI assistant, but the devices were designed to only start listening when prompted with a so-called wake word.When turned on, Bee devices are always recording. Amazon says this enables key features like conversation summaries and the ability to "review memories from the past few days to remember what you discussed." It can also track "trends or themes that recur" to give personalized goals or actions.With a Bee Pro subscription, which costs $12 per month, users can get unlimited conversation summaries and daily memories as well as integrations with Amazon's webstore, its Alexa+ AI assistant and third-party apps. For example, if a user mentions they need to buy dish soap, they might see the product recommended on the Amazon homepage, or in the Bee mobile and desktop apps.The company said Bee devices are designed so that "no one, including Amazon, can access your data." Users can delete their transcripts and summaries at any time and "no audio is ever stored," Amazon said. An LED light signals when Bee gadgets are recording, Amazon said. title: U.S. Treasury dismisses IMF debt warning and 'messy' forecasting
description: David Zervos, Chief Market Strategist of Jefferies LLC, speaks during an interview with CNBC on the floor at the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New
body: David Zervos, Chief Market Strategist of Jefferies LLC, speaks during an interview with CNBC on the floor at the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York City, U.S., September 3, 2025.Jeenah Moon | ReutersThe International Monetary Fund should check its own forecasting record before criticizing U.S. fiscal policy, David Zervos, newly appointed counselor to the Treasury Secretary, said on Thursday. "When we see pieces on the IMF, it's good to remember how messy their forecasts have been in the past," Zervos said in emailed comments to CNBC. The former Wall Street economist was responding to the IMF's Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva, who cautioned during the IMF-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok on Wednesday that strong U.S. economic growth would not be sufficient to put mounting federal debt on a sustainable course. Georgieva was herself responding to U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who told CNBC in August that the U.S. could "grow our way out" of a rising debt-to-GDP ratio, after government debt surpassed $40 trillion. watch now

schema.headline: U.S. Treasury dismisses IMF debt warning and 'messy' forecasting
